open_obligations: Note that the decomposition is developer-designed, not learned.
Check whether Reppert et al.'s tasks are hard in the sense of exceeding unaided human evaluation.
Check Reppert et al.'s own statement that all decompositions so far are fairly simple.
in.other_title: Iterated decomposition: human-in-the-loop workflow for refining compositional LM programs
in.rationale: Wu et al. ask whether decomposition beyond a fixed algorithmic tree is feasible for hard real-world tasks. Reppert et al. report a human-in-the-loop workflow that iteratively refines decompositions of science Q&A tasks, raising held-out accuracy (e.g. Qasper 38% to 69%); the decompositions are designed by developers, not learned by a model, so the 'learned' part of Wu et al.'s question stays open.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether task decompositions for hard real-world tasks can be found and improved, for science Q&A pipelines refined by human developers

text: The authors pose: is learning a task decomposition model, rather than using a fixed decomposition, feasible for hard real-world tasks? For what kinds of tasks is task decomposition fundamentally limiting? And how else can ML models assist humans in specifying preferences for high-level tasks?
title: Is learned task decomposition feasible for hard real-world tasks, and where does it fail?
